source_text:
Καὶ ὅσον βλέπει τις σιγῶντα ἐπίσκοπον, πλειόνως αὐτὸν φοβείσθω: πάντα γάρ, ὃν πέμπει ὁ οἰκοδεσπότης εἰς ἰδίαν οἰκονομίαν, οὕτως δεῖ ἡμᾶς αὐτὸν δέχεσθαι, ὡς αὐτὸν τὸν πέμψαντα, τὸν οὖν ἐπίσκοπον δῆλον ὅτι ὡς αὐτὸν κύριον δεῖ προσβλέπειν.
αὐτὸς μὲν οὖν Ὀνήσιμος ὑπερεπαινεῖ ὑμῶν τὴν ἐν θεῷ εὐταξίαν, ὅτι πάντες κατὰ ἀλήθειαν ζῆτε καὶ ὅτι ἐν ὑμῖν οὐδεμία αἵρεσις κατοικεῖ: ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ ἀκούετέ τινος πλέον, ἢ περὶ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ λαλοῦντος ἐν ἀληθείᾳ.
thought_title: Honor the bishop as the one sent by the master
orientation: Ignatius is writing to the church in Ephesus, urging them to honor their bishop Onesimus as they would the Lord himself.
pass_a_gloss: And as much as anyone sees a bishop being silent, let him fear him all the more. For everyone whom the master of the house sends for his own stewardship, thus it is necessary for us to receive him, as the one who sent him himself. The bishop therefore, it is clear, it is necessary to regard as the Lord himself. Onesimus himself, then, praises exceedingly your good order in God, because you all live according to truth and because no false teaching dwells among you. But neither do you listen to anyone more than to one speaking about Jesus Christ in truth.

choices.why: Keeps the participle's progressive force; the silence is the occasion for greater reverence, not a title
Renders the compound literally and preserves the household-stewardship image Ignatius is building
Keeps the possessive force of ἰδίαν and the purpose sense of εἰς
The compound verb intensifies the praise; a simple 'praises' loses the prefix
Keeps the prepositional phrase's location of the order as being in God, not merely godly
Uses the glossary term for αἵρεσις and keeps the vivid 'dwells' for κατοικεῖ

pass_b_english: The more you see a bishop keeping silence, the more you should revere him. For everyone whom the master of the house sends to manage his own household, we must receive as we would receive the one who sent him. Clearly, then, we must regard the bishop as the Lord himself.

Onesimus himself praises your good order in God beyond measure, because you all live according to truth and because no false teaching dwells among you. Nor do you listen to anyone more than to Jesus Christ speaking in truth.

last_rejected.why: ἰδίαν means 'his own' (the master's own), but 'for his own stewardship' is ambiguous—could mean bishop's own. The sense is 'into his own household management/administration'.
last_rejected.ruling: ἰδίαν refers to οἰκοδεσπότης; 'for his own stewardship' adequately conveys master's household management without meaningful ambiguity.

problems.quote: the more one sees a bishop being silent, the more let him fear him
problems.why: 'Fear' seems strong for silent bishop; may mean 'reverence' or 'be awed'.
problems.fix: Use 'revere' or note semantic range of phobeomai.

edits.old: the more let him fear him
edits.new: the more let him revere him

fixed: The English already says exactly what the source says for all other confirmed problems.

polish.changed: Clarified the implied subject 'you' in the opening sentence, smoothed the awkward 'being silent' to 'keeping silence,' clarified the household steward image, and made the transition between the two paragraphs clearer while preserving every claim and reference.

notes.quote: the more one sees a bishop being silent, the more let him revere him
notes.why: 'Being silent' seems to mean 'not speaking much' or 'being reserved,' but could mean 'in his silent authority.'
notes.fix: Note: refers to bishop's dignified reserve, not muteness.

polish.changed: Clarified that Onesimus is the bishop being discussed, kept the silence phrase as 'keeping silence' to preserve the source's ambiguity, and made the pronoun references explicit.

notes.why: Onesimus called 'bishop' twice, then just 'Onesimus' without title.

notes.quote: the more you see a bishop keeping silence, the more you should revere him
notes.why: 'Keeping silence' = refraining from speech? Or 'living quietly'?
